Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: skip SW interception for font files to prevent crash in OnlyOffice v7.5

When fonts are not yet cached, the SW's async caches.match() adds latency
to font requests. During WASM initialization (high CPU load), this extra
latency triggers Chrome's font-loading intervention, which causes OnlyOffice
v7.5 to crash with "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'units_per_EM')"
when its fallback font object is not fully initialized.

Skipping SW interception for font files restores the pre-SW behavior and
lets the browser cache fonts natively.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: apply ASC.ttf font fallback to slide and word sdk

Commit 91bc4e2 patched cell/sdk-all.js to use || q['ASC.ttf'] as a
fallback when a font is not yet loaded in the font cache (q). The same
pattern existed in slide/sdk-all.js (A.Ya) and word/sdk-all.js (A.Za)
but was not patched, causing an uncaught TypeError:
  "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'units_per_EM')"

This crash was triggered when AllFonts.js mapped Windows font paths to
local files that hadn't finished loading, making q[fontName] undefined.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: use null guard instead of ASC.ttf fallback for font metrics

The previous || q['ASC.ttf'] fallback caused all fonts with unloaded
metrics to inherit ASC.ttf's dimensions (units_per_EM, ascender, etc.),
resulting in chaotic rendering for PPT/DOCX.

Replace with an early return when the font is not yet in the cache.
This skips metric setup for that render cycle — yUc stays 0 so the
block retries next frame — without corrupting layout with wrong values.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: apply null guard to cell sdk font metrics (same as slide/word)

The || q['ASC.ttf'] fallback added in 91bc4e2 had the same flaw as in
slide and word: it would use ASC.ttf metrics for any unloaded font,
corrupting cell layout. Replace with an early return instead.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix: use canvas fallback mode when font not yet loaded in slide/word sdk

When the font is missing from q (not yet loaded), the previous fixes
caused two failure modes:
- || q['ASC.ttf']: wrong family_name → canvas renders all text as SimSun → font chaos
- if (!K) return: c2b never set → falls through to HarfBuzz path → a.Tce crash

The c2b flag controls the render path in $P:
  true  → Canvas 2D fallback (safe, uses family_name for font string)
  false → HarfBuzz shaping (crashes when font handle not initialized)

When K is undefined, force canvas mode (c2b=true) with yUc=2048 as a
placeholder so the if(0==yUc) block does not re-enter this cycle.
Cna (family_name) stays unset, so canvas falls back to SimSun for this
render cycle only — retried fresh on the next $P call after WYc() resets.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

revert: restore sdkjs files to pre-91bc4e2 state

The changes in 91bc4e2 introduced:
1. AllFonts.js: mapped Windows font paths to large local files
   (NotoSansTC-VF.ttf 11.4MB), which caused A.Ya to be non-null
   so the ?? 'ASC.ttf' fallback never triggered, leading to crashes
2. cell/sdk-all.js: added || q['ASC.ttf'] to paper over the crash,
   but this set wrong family_name causing font rendering chaos
3. slide/sdk-all.js and word/sdk-all.js: were left unpatched,
   later patched by us but with cascading HarfBuzz errors

Restoring pre-91bc4e2 state: Windows font paths fail to load,
A.Ya is null/undefined, ?? 'ASC.ttf' fallback applies naturally,
matching the stable v0.0.3 behavior.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 4.6 <noreply@anthropic.com>

OnlyOffice v7.5 units_per_EM crash:

- Document URLs (?src=, ?file=) bypass the cache to stay fresh
- Cross-origin and non-GET requests are not intercepted

fix(v7): Safari idle-callback polyfill + readonly preview mode

- #84: polyfill requestIdleCallback/cancelIdleCallback in the v7 iframe
  patch. v7 SDK calls requestIdleCallback() bare; old Safari has no such
  global and throws ReferenceError during init. Patch runs before SDK in
  each editor iframe, so defining it on window covers all bare calls.
- #25/#85/#87: wire ?readonly=true (also ?readonly=1, bare ?readonly)
  for pure preview mode — openDocumentFromUrl already accepts readonly,
  index.ts just wasn't parsing it.
- #25: give editorConfig a default Guest user so the SDK's getInitials()
  never receives a blank name (which crashed anonymous preview).

#12/#15/#92 (HiDPI/cursor) intentionally NOT changed: v7 has no
AscDesktopEditor, so the SDK uses native devicePixelRatio; the v9
GetSupportedScaleValues shim would install a fake desktop path here.

See docs/explorations/2026-06-23-v7-issue-backport.md.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.8 <noreply@anthropic.com>

feat(agent): Phase 1.3 runtime — tool-use loop ties tools to the LLM

runtime.ts closes the loop between the tool layer and an LLM provider:
- toLLMToolDefs(): AgentTool registry → LLMToolDef[].
- runAgent(provider, userMessage, opts): chat → if the model requests tools,
  execute each and feed tool_result blocks back → chat again → until the model
  stops calling tools or maxIterations (default 8) is hit. Returns
  {text, messages, toolCallCount, stoppedOnLimit} and emits onEvent progress.

Errors don't break the loop: unknown tool or a thrown tool error becomes an
isError tool_result the model can see and react to. Provider-agnostic and
editor-agnostic, so fully unit-tested with a scripted provider + mock tools.

feat(agent): streaming output (Anthropic + WebLLM)

Plan step 3. Assistant replies render token-by-token instead of arriving as
one block.

Architecture: LLMProvider gains an OPTIONAL chatStream(messages, tools, onDelta)
that emits text deltas and resolves the same LLMResponse as chat(); the runtime
uses it when present and transparently falls back to chat() otherwise. Streamed
turns surface as assistant_delta events plus a final assistant event flagged
streamed:true.

UI: AgentChatControllerOptions gains onAgentDelta/onAgentStreamEnd; the panel
maintains a single live bubble that deltas append into and closes on turn end.
A streamed turn isn't re-emitted as a separate agent turn — but a consumer that
wires no delta handler still gets the whole turn, so text is never lost.

Providers: Anthropic via the SDK messages.stream() (.on('text') + finalMessage),
WebLLM via create({stream:true}) folded by a new shared accumulateOpenAIStream
(reassembles tool_calls by index) back through parseOpenAIResponse. Both default
providers (cloud Anthropic, offline WebLLM) now stream; OpenAI/Ollama fall back
to non-streaming for now (raw-fetch SSE parsing deferred — the accumulator is

feat(agent): Gemini provider

Plan step 4. Adds a Google Gemini cloud provider (browser Direct Mode).

Gemini's REST shape differs structurally from the neutral (Anthropic-style,
id-keyed) model — it matches tool results to calls by function *name*. So the
converters build an id→name map from assistant tool_use blocks and resolve each
tool_result's name from it; parseGeminiResponse synthesises a stable id
(name-partIndex) per functionCall so the runtime can still pair results. Tool
outputs wrap as functionResponse objects; empty-property schemas drop their
parameters (Gemini rejects them); the tools field is omitted when none.

Wiring: factory branch + ProviderOptions; panel gains the option and a
CLOUD_PROVIDERS set replacing the scattered anthropic||openai checks; key stored
under agent_api_key_gemini and sent via the x-goog-api-key header; i18n (zh/en).
Non-streaming for now (like OpenAI/Ollama).

feat: auto-reload on SW update + privacy-friendly Cloudflare analytics

Two independent changes to the standalone app entry:

1. SW freshness — after a deploy the new service worker skipWaiting()s and
   claims clients but never reloads the already-rendered page, so users keep
   seeing the previously-cached build until a manual refresh (the "refresh once
   more and it's fixed" symptom, which is what surfaced the stale PPTX font
   bug). index.ts now reloads once on `controllerchange`, guarded so it fires
   only on a real update (not first install), only once, and never while a
   document is open (a reload would discard unsaved edits).

2. Analytics — add cookieless Cloudflare Web Analytics (lib/analytics.ts)
   instead of Google Analytics, to stay consistent with the local-only privacy
   pitch (no cookies, no consent banner). The beacon loads only when a token
   (VITE_CF_BEACON_TOKEN) is set AND the app is top-level (never in embed
   iframe). With no token the whole beacon path is tree-shaken out, so the
   default build ships tracking-free. pages-build-site.yml injects the token
   from a repo variable.

Verified end-to-end with chrome-devtools: first-install no reload, update
reload once, doc-open no reload; beacon injects top-level, absent in embed,
absent (tree-shaken) with no token. lint:ts + sw-routing tests + build pass.

feat(converter): load x2t WASM from gzip, unblock Cloudflare Pages migration

CF Pages rejects files >25 MiB at deploy; the raw x2t.wasm is 55 MB. Ship
only the ~11 MB x2t.wasm.gz and decompress it in the browser, handing the
bytes to Emscripten via Module.wasmBinary (which then skips its own fetch of
x2t.wasm entirely).

- prepareWasmBinary(): fetch .gz -> detect gzip magic (1f 8b) -> decompress
  with native DecompressionStream('gzip') only when still compressed. Some
  servers (Vite dev/preview) send Content-Encoding: gzip and the browser has
  already decompressed it (bytes start with \0asm); static hosts (CF/GitHub
  Pages) send raw gzip. The magic-byte check handles both.
- Drop public/wasm/x2t/x2t.wasm (55M) and x2t.wasm.br (8M); keep .gz + x2t.js.

Verified: both decompression branches compile a valid 54.7M wasm; Playwright
integration confirms x2t runtime initializes and zero requests hit the raw
x2t.wasm; dist has no file >25 MiB; lint + 240 tests pass.

fix(embed): send Editor.bin verbatim as a latin1 string, not base64-wrapped (#113)

The previous attempt (18bb045) base64-encoded the whole bin before
sending asc_openDocument. But x2t already emits Editor.bin as an ASCII
text container ("DOCY;v5;<len>;<base64>"), and the SDK identifies a
string buf by literally checking its first characters against

sniff fail: silent "Loading document" hang in Chrome, error -85 in the
reporter's Qt WebEngine environment.

Send the bin bytes verbatim as a latin1 string instead (chunked
String.fromCharCode, no btoa). Strings still survive postMessage in
hosts that corrupt ArrayBuffers, which was the point of the original
fix, and the DOCY signature stays intact.

fix(v9): images no longer hang the save pipeline -- serverless image registration

Root cause, proven with an offline Node repro of the exact x2t.wasm
call: with no Document Server, sendImgUrls registers nothing, the DOCY
writers embed the image's raw external URL (getImageLocal misses), and
x2t.wasm loops forever on such a path -- the same DOCY converts in
about 100ms once the path is a registered media name. prepareEditorIframe
gains a fourth guard: a self-healing getImageLocal that registers
external ids at serialization time, a serverless sendImgUrls honoring
the server response contract, and a convertFromBin medias fallback that
materializes the registered bytes into the WASM FS. The formerly-hanging
insert-image-then-save flow now completes in ~130ms with the image bytes
present in the output, and a permanent embed-regression case guards it.

fix(v9): make the toolbar Save button and Ctrl+S actually save -- serverless save semantics

Root cause of "Save is always grey": the SDK's coauthoring autosave loop
(40ms tick, autoSaveGapFast 2s) pushes every edit to a Document Server
and, on the fake success a serverless build produces, marks history as
saved -- isDocumentCanSave flips true then back to false 1-2s after each

the user cannot save. Even when it briefly enabled, asc_Save took the
coauthoring path and produced no file. Guard 5 in prepareEditorIframe:
zero the autosave gap (and pin asc_setAutoSaveGap so the app layer's
settings re-apply cannot resurrect it), and route user-initiated
asc_Save to asc_DownloadAs in the document's own format so the existing
onlyoffice-file-stream save UX runs. Autosave-flagged calls keep the
original path. New embed-regression case types into a cell, asserts the
button stays enabled past the old gap, and asserts asc_Save yields the
file stream.

fix(v9): cache the indexed font catalog and x2t wasm -- CJK decks no longer sit on "Loading presentation" for minutes on production

Root cause of "opens instantly on localhost, loads forever on
edit.chaxus.com": the editor's indexed fonts (/fonts/NNN, no extension,
200 KB - 5 MB each) had no Cache-Control rule, so Cloudflare Pages served
them max-age=0 / cf-cache-status DYNAMIC, and in the service worker they
missed the .ttf/.woff skip and fell into stale-while-revalidate whose
`cache: 'no-cache'` revalidation re-downloaded every one on every open.
The SDK loads document fonts through a serial queue; a real Chinese deck
pulled 32 files / 37.6 MB (20 of them the Word/Slide "default fonts"
Arial/Times/Courier x 4 faces the document never uses), and measured
per-file times climbed 3s -> 89s -> 165s -> 214s+ while
isDocumentLoadComplete stayed false. Fix: _headers pins /fonts/* and
x2t.wasm.gz as immutable (they only change with a vendor swap, which
also changes the referencing HTML; editor JS/HTML is deliberately NOT
pinned since some of it carries our runtime patches), and the SW serves
those two shapes cache-first instead of revalidating. Same 3-layer
lesson as the campaign harness: production adds the CDN + SW layers that
localhost never exercises.

perf(v9): guard 8 -- parallel font prefetch and no default-font preload

The vendor's CFontLoader works fonts_loading strictly one family at a
time (request the faces of [0], poll every 50ms, shift, repeat), so a
real Chinese deck's 30 families cost 30 serial multi-MB round trips --
minutes on a cold CDN path even after the caching fix. Guard 8 wraps
LoadDocumentFonts / LoadDocumentFonts2 to kick off LoadFontAsync for
every still-unloaded face of every queued family right after the vendor
enqueues them (LoadFontAsync is idempotent per file), so the browser
downloads them in parallel and the serial poll finds each already in
flight; measured dispatch spread for 30 fonts drops from minutes to
3 ms. It also turns IsNeedDefaultFonts off: Word/Slide preloaded
Arial/Symbol/Wingdings/Courier/Times (12 files, 3.2 MB) on every open
"just in case", while the runtime path already fetches any of them on
first actual use. New embed-regression case pins both.

fix(v9): retry an open once when the editor, not the document, failed (#144)

The vendor's open path awaits AscCommon.x2t.convertToBin with no catch, and
x2t_helper rewraps every throw as "Document conversion failed: ...", so a
half-initialised editor and a genuinely broken document both reach the user
as the same -82 "the file is corrupted or unsupported". The font system is
the concrete offender: fetchFonts iterates AscFonts.g_font_infos and
dereferences g_font_loader.fontFiles[i].Id with no readiness check of its
own, while both are populated concurrently with the document load. Whoever
wins depends on cache warmth and CPU, which is why the reporter's file opens
in a freshly installed Edge and fails in the Chrome they use all day, and why
creating a document (no convertToBin at all) is unaffected.

- isFontSystemReady(): the existing fetchFonts guard only checked
  g_font_infos; require the font files too and import without fonts until
  both are up.
- classifyOpenFailure(): x2t verdicts on the bytes (conversion code, an
  emscripten Aborted, a missing importer) stay immediate errors; boot-state
  TypeErrors, a missing x2t module and failed fetches are environment
  failures.
- An environment failure rebuilds the editor once with the same bytes before
  anything is reported; open generations keep the superseded frame's late
  duplicate rejections off the document that replaced it.
- The -82 toast now carries the underlying reason, so the next report is
  diagnosable from its screenshot alone.

Tests: unit coverage for both predicates; test/e2e/open-retry.spec.ts injects
the boot-state failure into the first convertToBin of a real editor session
and asserts the document opens and still saves, while open-failure.spec pins
the no-retry side.

fix(v9): await the font system instead of importing without it (#144)

The first guard answered an unready font system with cb([]) -- a fontless
import. That turned the crash into a degradation but left the race in place:
whether the open conversion sees a built font system still depended on cache
warmth. Order the two instead. awaitFontSystem holds the vendor's fetchFonts
callback until AscFonts.g_font_infos and g_font_loader.fontFiles are both
populated, then delegates to the vendor implementation, so the conversion runs
with real fonts rather than around them.

The wait is bounded and measured, because both risks are real:

- Cost: a ready font system delegates synchronously and schedules nothing. A
  warm local open waits ~200 ms, which is itself the proof of the race (warm
  caches let x2t start before the fonts land); a cold profile waits zero, the
  fonts being ready ~1 s before the x2t module. open-retry.spec records the
  real number and fails if it ever exceeds 2 s, so an environment where fonts
  systematically lose cannot silently add seconds to every open.
- Font loading failures: individual font downloads are already swallowed by
  the vendor's own fetchFonts. A font catalog that never arrives times out
  after 5 s and falls back to exactly the previous behaviour -- a fontless
  import, never a hang.

fix(v9): never leave the conversion waiting on a callback that will not come (#144)

Review finding on the previous commit. The try/catch that keeps a dead realm
from throwing out of the timer also wrapped the handover to the vendor's
fetchFonts -- and that function throws synchronously: it walks
AscFonts.g_font_infos and dereferences g_font_loader.fontFiles[index].Id, so a
font system that is up but incomplete is a TypeError, not a clean return.

x2t_helper settles the conversion only from inside the callback
(new Promise(resolve => AscCommon.fetchFonts(cb))). Swallowing that throw
without answering the callback therefore does not degrade the open, it hangs
it: no rejection, so no -82, no failure guard, no retry -- the permanent
spinner installOpenFailureGuard exists to prevent.

The synchronous path stays unguarded on purpose: it runs inside the caller's
promise executor, where a throw becomes a rejected open and the guard retries
it. Only the timer path, which has no such executor, now falls back to the
fontless import it already uses for a timed-out wait. isFontSystemReady and
the wait probe move inside the try as well -- a throw there escaped the timer
too, and skipped clearInterval, leaving a poll running forever.

Reverse-verified: without the cb([]) fallback the new test reports the
callback was never called (i.e. the hang); without the read guard the dead
realm throws straight out of advanceTimersByTime.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

ci: bound every job and stop apt from hanging the whole pipeline

Four CI runs in one day were killed at GitHub's six-hour job limit, each one
stalled at exactly the same point: apt-get, inside `playwright install
--with-deps`, going silent right after fetching the release indexes. All three
e2e jobs run that same step, so a different job hung each time and it read as
general flakiness rather than one cause. Every one of them blocked a pull
request until it was re-run by hand.

Nothing bounded it. ci.yml -- the workflow behind four of the six required
checks -- had no timeout-minutes on any job, while the newer smoke and nightly
workflows all did. apt enforces no wall-clock limit of its own, so a mirror
that accepts the connection and then sends nothing can stall until the
platform intervenes.

- .github/scripts/install-playwright.sh wraps each install attempt in
  `timeout` and retries three times. A stalled apt-get is a grandchild of the
  timed-out process and survives it, so the retry first kills it by process
  name (matching the full command line would match the sudo running it and
  take out the script instead) and clears the dpkg locks it left behind --
  without that the retry fails instantly on "Could not get lock".
- .github/actions/setup collapses the nine copies of the pnpm/Node/install
  block, eight of which inlined their own browser install. Browsers are cached
  against the Playwright version rather than the lockfile, so a dependency bump
  no longer re-downloads them.
- Every job in all eight workflows gets a timeout, sized at two to three times
  its measured runtime. A hang now costs fifteen minutes, not an evening.
- ci.yml drops the run for a superseded pull request commit; runs for main are
  never cancelled, since a deploy and the production smoke judge that commit.
- release.yml installed a pnpm workspace with `npm install`, which cannot
  resolve the four `workspace:*` dependencies in the root manifest; it now uses
  the shared setup.

test/unit/workflow-contract.test.ts pins all of it: no job without a timeout,
no workflow inlining a browser install, and the retry and lock cleanup the
script depends on. Verified in reverse -- removing each guard turns it red.

ci: pin the wrangler compatibility date so the calendar cannot break the build

Since 00:00 UTC today the e2e-pages job failed on every branch, main included,
without a line of code changing. wrangler is started with no compatibility date
and no config file, so it defaults to today's date -- and the workerd binary it
ships only supports dates up to its own release:

  This Worker requires compatibility date "2026-08-19", but the newest date
  supported by this server binary is "2026-08-18".

A value that arrives on a calendar rather than in a commit fails everywhere at
once and looks nothing like its cause, so pin it. Any date the installed
workerd knows will do: old dates are supported indefinitely and this project
serves static assets with no Pages Functions.

The failure also reached CI wearing a disguise. The serve command was an
unconditional restart loop, there because workerd does die mid-run when a
browser aborts a large download and a crash should cost one retried test rather
than the job. But it could not tell a server that crashed from one that never
started, so it retried the startup error once a second until Playwright gave up
with "Timed out waiting 300000ms from config.webServer" -- the real message
sitting fifteen repetitions upstream. It now gives up after three attempts that
each died inside ten seconds, and still restarts a server that had been up.

Both live in bin/serve-pages-dev.sh: shell belongs in bin/, not inside a
template literal where every shell variable has to dodge interpolation.

Verified against the real wrangler locally: reproduced the failure, confirmed
the pinned date starts and serves 200, confirmed the give-up path exits on a
server that never starts and that a crash after ten seconds still only
restarts.

fix(docker): ship a cache contract so a pulled image actually reaches the browser (#144)

static-web-server does not read dist/_headers -- that format is Cloudflare
Pages' -- so the self-hosted image fell back to its extension-based defaults:
max-age=86400 for HTML and max-age=31536000 for every stable-named .js/.css,
none of it revalidated. A self-hoster who pulled a new image therefore kept
serving the previous editor.html out of the browser cache, and the hashed
bundle it points at was cached for a year alongside it, so neither file ever
touched the server: the page ran entirely on the old build. That is how the
reporter on #144 re-pulled the image and got a byte-identical error -- the fix
shipped the day before was not running at all.

sws.toml is the Docker twin of public/_headers: revalidate by default (a 304,
not a re-download -- the server answers conditional requests), long-lived only
for content-addressed names and the vendor-versioned binaries.

Also close the diagnostic gap that made the report unreadable in the first
place. The vendor installs its own window.onerror/onunhandledrejection in the
editor frame and turns ANY error that lands before the document is loaded into
asc_onError(-82, Critical) -- the same code and the same dialog our conversion
guard raises. installOpenFailureGuard only recorded messages matching the
conversion pattern, so every other failure produced a toast with a bare number.
It now keeps the first pre-ready frame error (skipping extension and
cross-origin scripts, as the vendor's own filter does), names it in the -82
toast, and marks the document as failed so a save after a vendor-reported open
failure is refused immediately instead of waiting out its timeout.

asserts the headers on the real container (E2E_DOCKER=1);

fix(x2t): open documents on browsers that refuse the engine's memory (#144)

x2t asks the browser for 283 MB of committed heap and a 2 GB address-space
reservation, per editor frame, and #144 is a reporter whose two Chromes refuse
while Edge accepts on the same machines -- in a fresh incognito window, on the
first open. Four things came out of that.

The peak. The engine is now compiled straight off the network through
emscripten's own instantiateWasm hook, so the 40.2 MB inflated module never
exists as a buffer at the moment WebAssembly is asking for the heap. Engines
that cannot stream still take the buffered path, and that copy is released at
calledRun -- BOTH references, including x2t.js's own top-level `var
wasmBinary`, without which the release freed nothing.

The verdict. A refused allocation aborts x2t before it is instantiated, so it
never saw the bytes -- but the `Aborted(` rule classified it as a verdict on
the document: no retry, and a toast telling the reader their file may be
corrupt. It is now an environment failure, retried like the others, and the
toast says what was refused (reservation or commit) and on what build. An x2t
exit code still wins, even when it mentions memory: that one IS a verdict.

The number. 283 MB is not a tunable -- measured, tried and reverted: static
and BSS reach ~267 MB, so a smaller `initial` puts the module's own compile-time
pointers outside its memory. bin/x2t-memory-report.mjs is how to re-measure
after a vendor bump; the toast interpolates the figure from the binary rather
than carrying eight hand-written copies of it.

The download. x2t.wasm.gz is recompressed with zopfli --i15: 377 KB off the
largest asset in the app, byte-identical once inflated. The contract pins the
hash of the DECOMPRESSED module, so provenance is not tied to a compressor.

fix(sw): let a deploy reach visitors without every tab closing first (#144)

A fixed bug could look unchanged after an upgrade because the fix was never
delivered: the new worker installed and then waited indefinitely. Two causes,
and both had to go.

Nothing asked for the switch. The route split (2026-08-16) moved the landing
page to `/`, which ships no editor bundle, so the promotion in lib/sw-update.ts
only ever ran on `/editor` -- where the open starts before the registration
resolves, leaving `hasOpenDocument()` true every time. `/zh-CN/` registered no
worker at all. public/sw-register.js is the missing half: the landing pages
register the worker and promote a waiting one, covering all three ways an
install can arrive (already waiting, mid-install, or installed before the
`updatefound` listener existed -- `statechange` reports none of the last).

And every deploy looked like an engine replacement. The runtime cache was named
after the build, so activating always meant discarding the outgoing build's
sdkjs / web-apps / fonts -- which an open editor still lazy-loads from. It is
now named after the vendor CONTENT (bin/build.sh hashes the served trees), so
the common deploy -- app changed, vendor did not -- shares the cache, discards
nothing, and takes over during install. Whether it may is decided by what the
other runtime caches CONTAIN, not by their names: by name the check fails on
the very deploy that introduces it, which is also the one deploy the
client-count handshake cannot work on, and #144 would have stayed undeliverable.

The cost of content-naming is that nothing clears the cache any more, so
activate() prunes the outgoing build's /assets/<hash> -- but only with no
window of that build open, since an editor with a document is deliberately not
reloaded and those files exist nowhere else. The trim evicts app assets before
vendor ones for the same reason: `keys[0]` was the oldest entry, i.e. exactly
the multi-MB binaries the cache-first branch was added to protect.

feat(history): add the local document history store

The storage layer for autosave snapshots, written to its final shape now
rather than as a single-document special case: a recovery bar today and a
paged, searchable history page next both read these records, and simplifying
now would mean a rewrite plus a migration later.

Metadata and bytes live in separate object stores. The list view reads
hundreds of small rows and never touches a megabyte, which is what keeps it
usable once a library exists.

Retention is part of the write, not a chore for later. Snapshots arrive on
their own schedule, so an unbounded database ends with the browser refusing a
write -- and the write it refuses is the edit the user wanted back. Each
document keeps three revisions; the library keeps to min(500 MB, half the
reported quota) and evicts whole documents by least-recently-opened.
QuotaExceededError means "make room and try once", never a crash: browsers
grant very different amounts of room and evict behind our back.

Snapshots are stored as typed arrays rather than Blobs. The bytes arrive from
the editor frame as an ArrayBuffer and go back as one, so a Blob only adds a
wrap in and an async unwrap out -- and typed arrays are the shape structured
clone round-trips faithfully everywhere.

Titles are searched in memory. An IndexedDB key range can only match a
prefix, which rules out substrings and any Chinese title; metadata rows are
under a kilobyte, so scanning them is both simpler and more capable.

Reverse-verified, each independently turning exactly one case red: removing
the revision trim, the budget eviction, the blob clear in clearAllHistory, and
the quota retry.

feat(history): autosave recovery points and offer them on the next boot

Snapshots are taken by the app's own metronome, not the SDK's autosave loop --
that loop is switched off on purpose, because with no document server behind
it a fake save success greys out the Save button forever.

The beat is slow by design. One snapshot is a full export: the SDK serialises,
x2t converts behind its 283 MB heap request, and the bytes cross the frame
boundary. Editors whose snapshot is a JSON.stringify write on every keystroke;
this one waits for something to save, a lull in the typing, and time since the
last snapshot. visibilitychange -> hidden gets one more, which is the last
moment that reliably has time to run -- beforeunload does not, and a phone
being task-switched away never sees one.

A Web Lock keeps two tabs off one document. Without it both would autosave
and take turns overwriting each other, interleaving two divergent documents
into a single row -- worse than having no history at all.

The offer on the next boot is the other half: a snapshot nobody is told about
is not a recovery. It follows WordPress's framing rather than "you have a
backup" -- what matters is which copy is ahead, so the bar names the document
and when its edits happened, and only appears when the snapshot is newer than
the last time bytes reached the disk. Dismissing is remembered until the
document changes again.

Restoring goes back in through the ordinary local-file path with the history
id attached, so editing continues that row instead of starting a duplicate.

Reverse-verified: ignoring dismissals, ignoring savedToDiskAt, and dropping
the history id from the restore each turn exactly one case red.

Revert "fix(fonts): replace 171 MB of proprietary faces, and give each script one family"

This reverts commit 6dd918f. It broke text rendering on the live site: every
glyph came out shifted, so typing "Hello" put "Fcjjm" on the page and the
style gallery showed "标题 E" where it should read "标题 1". CJK rendered as
blank. Reverting first; the licensing work returns once it renders.

What the sweep got wrong is the swap mechanism, not the font choices.
`__fonts_infos` rows were repointed at a replacement's existing position --
"Arial" made to share Liberation Sans's position, every Chinese family made
to share the new Noto CJK one. The engine builds one font object per position
in `__fonts_files`, and a position turns out to be an identity it will not
share: two families on one position renders from the wrong glyph indices.

Established by bisection against a local build of the exact vendor tree:

- sweep applied              -> "Fcjjm", CJK blank
- ranges index口径 corrected -> unchanged (so not the ASCW3 off-by-one)
- waited 70s, face Status=0  -> unchanged (so not a load-time race)
- indices untouched, only the *bytes* of Arial's four slots replaced with
  Liberation Sans -> "Hello ABC 你好" renders correctly

Glyph order is not the culprit either: Arial and Liberation Sans agree on
every codepoint checked, digits included (0->19, 1->20, H->43, e->72).

The fix is to keep every row's index exactly as it is and swap the file
*contents* instead, with families that cannot afford their own copy of a
16 MB CJK face dropping to no face at all so they fall through the range
table. That lands separately, verified in a browser before it ships.

Nothing in the E2E suite caught this: the visual cases compare an original
against its own save round trip, and both sides render with the same wrong
font, so the pixels match. A case that types text and reads it back is part
of the follow-up.

feat(save): write back into the document's own file instead of downloading a copy

Every save went through a "save as" dialog and threw the handle away, so saving
twice meant choosing the same file twice -- and the second choice raised the
browser's "a file with that name already exists" prompt. Keeping the handle
turns that into what a desktop editor does: the first save picks the file,
every save after it writes to that file.

It is also the strongest privacy answer this app has. A document that goes back
to the user's own file system needs no copy in the browser at all -- the local
history exists precisely because, until now, there was nowhere else for the
work to be.

Handles are stored per document id, in a new store in the same database, so the
link survives closing the tab. They are held in memory for the session as well:
that keeps saving free between reloads, and keeps the feature working while
IndexedDB is not (a private window, a full disk) for as long as the tab lives.

Everything that can go wrong falls back to the download the app already did,
and forgets the handle on the way: the file was moved or deleted, permission
was refused, the API is absent. Forgetting doubles as the way to save
somewhere else -- the next save offers the picker again. A dismissed picker is
a decision, not a failure, so it does not download a copy the user just
declined.

Chromium only. Safari has no local-disk picker and Firefox has said it will not
add one, so this is strictly an upgrade over the existing behaviour.

`?doc=` is renamed `?saved=`: the old name read as "docx", and the parameter is
not about a format but about which of this browser's saved documents to open.
It stays a query parameter rather than becoming a path segment on purpose --
Google Docs and Figma put ids in the path because those ids name something on a
server anyone with the link can open, while this one names a row in one
browser's IndexedDB. In a path it would look shareable, and whoever received it
would open an empty editor.

E2E stubs the picker with a real origin-private file handle rather than a
hand-made object, so the handle genuinely round-trips through structured clone
into IndexedDB the way a disk handle does -- a fake object cannot, and that
round trip is the feature. Reverse-verified: not remembering the handle turns
both cases red.

perf(history): derive the snapshot interval from what an export actually costs

The 90 s interval was a guess dressed up as a constant: "exports are expensive"
with no number behind it. Measured it (bin/export-benchmark.mjs, added here),
and the guess was an order of magnitude off.

Desktop, x2t already loaded: 42 ms for a one-page docx, 51 ms at 200
paragraphs, 87 ms at 2000, 59 ms for a 1k-row workbook, 123 ms for 20k rows.
Snapshots are 25-486 KB. The first export of a session costs ~1.2 s, but that
is loading x2t and is paid once, not per snapshot.

So 90 s was far too cautious on a desktop -- and 30 s would be too aggressive
on a phone, where the same export runs several times slower on a device already
closer to losing its canvas (#145). One number cannot be right for both.

The interval is now clamp(lastExportMs x 300, 30 s, 180 s): spend a fixed 1/300
of wall-clock time exporting, and let the device decide by being fast or slow.
42 ms earns 12.6 s and takes the 30 s floor; 123 ms earns 36.9 s on its own;
600 ms on a slow phone backs off to the 180 s ceiling. No device detection, no
UA sniffing, and it stays correct for hardware that does not exist yet.

Also tightened the e2e window that waits for a snapshot from 45 s to 25 s. It
was chosen against the old 90 s interval; with a 30 s floor the periodic tick
would fit inside 45 s again and the case would pass whether or not the branch
it names does anything -- the same trap this spec fell into once already.

test(save): wait for the save to finish instead of racing it

The spec reads back the file the stubbed picker handed the app, and it was
polling that file's contents from the moment it pressed Ctrl+S. A save does
not edit the file in place -- it writes elsewhere and swaps the result in when
the stream closes -- so a snapshot taken before the swap is dead after it, and
a read straddling one fails with NotReadableError. expect.poll does not retry
a callback that throws, so a read one beat too early was reported as a file
that could not be read: PR #177, eight readme files, went red on the Docker
shard, where two workers on four cores make the timing likelier.

Count the writes instead of guessing when they end. The stub wraps
createWritable on the prototype -- not on the handle it hands out, because the
second page's handle was rebuilt out of IndexedDB, which is the thing this
spec exists to prove -- and tracks how many streams are open and how many have
closed. Every read now waits for the save it asked for to have committed with
nothing open on the file, so there is no window left to land in rather than a
smaller one.

That also buys an assertion the content polling could not make: two saves
write exactly twice. Nothing but a save may open that file.

No product change: lib/save-target.ts opens one writable per save.

test(history): read the history database through one guarded reader

Three specs each opened `document-history` by hand to check what autosave
stored, and only one of them did it safely. A versionless indexedDB.open on a
database that does not exist yet creates an empty version 1 with no object
stores -- the app creates its stores at version 2 -- and asking that for
`docs` throws inside the onsuccess handler, where nothing is listening. The
promise never settles, so the connection is never closed, and the leaked
connection then blocks the app's own upgrade, so the snapshot the spec is
waiting for can never be written. The spec fails 60 seconds later saying a
snapshot never appeared, which is true by then, and reads as an autosave bug.

That state -- database not there yet -- is precisely the state a spec is in
while it waits for the first snapshot, so this was one lost race away in
save-to-file and history-page.

autosave-recovery already had the right shape: check objectStoreNames, close
on every path, handle onupgradeneeded and the query's onerror. Move it to
test/e2e/lib/history-db.ts and have all three use it, so the next spec that
needs to read history does not have to rediscover any of this.

Verified: with the database absent, the old shape logs an uncaught
NotFoundError, never settles, and leaves a connection that makes the app's
version-2 open fire onblocked; the guarded one resolves empty and the app
opens and creates its stores.

A user opened a new spreadsheet and got a card in the corner offering to
restore New_Document.docx -- a different document, from two hours earlier --
with its primary button clipped off the card's edge. Their verdict: the prompt

/editor never opens empty: a bare visit is redirected to the landing page, so
every boot is a boot with a document arriving. The card appeared 1.5 s later
and excluded only the document named by ?saved=, which means it could only ever
land on top of a document the user had just opened, to talk about a different
one. There is no timing or wording that fixes that, because the editor has no
quiet moment for an announcement to arrive in.

interrupting anyone: the homepage's "continue last time" line, which is where
the common return visit actually lands, and /history. The recovery feature
itself is untouched -- restoreDocument still puts the newest snapshot back
through the ordinary open path, and ?saved=<id> still restores on reload. Only
the unsolicited announcement is gone, along with getRecoverableDoc,
dismissRecovery and the dismissedAt field that existed to remember declining an
offer that no longer exists.

The same reasoning removes one more: opening a document in a second tab raised
a warning that another tab was editing it. The user did nothing wrong, has
nothing to do about it, and which tab holds the write lock is our bookkeeping.
The lock stays -- two tabs writing snapshots would interleave two divergent
histories -- but it is silent now.

What survives is written down in the exploration doc, with the rule that
separates them: an answer to something the user did is not an interruption; an
announcement about something we did is. "Autosave stopped, you are out of

fix(fonts): replace the 79 proprietary faces, by moving rows instead of files

The vendor bundle arrived with the font set an OnlyOffice *server* picks up
from its host: Microsoft's core web fonts, Monotype's Arial/Times/Courier and
~150 MB of Chinese faces owned by SinoType, Founder, ZhongYi, GreatWall and
Stone. 79 files, 171 MB, redistributed from a public repository and a public
origin. They are gone; every name a document can reference still resolves.

The first attempt (#170) was reverted within the hour (#174) because the live
site came back with every glyph shifted -- `Hello` drawn as `Fcjjm` -- and the
note written afterwards concluded that substitution was impossible on this
vendor without rebuilding four coupled datasets. That conclusion was wrong.
There is one rule, and the pristine vendor catalog satisfies it at all 267 of
its referenced positions:

  the family name inside the file at position P must belong to a row that
  points at P.

The engine reads `m_pFaceInfo.family_name` off the face it loaded and resolves
*that* through the matcher again (sdk-all.js, StringShaper.Shape), so a
position holding a file that calls itself something else gets shaped by one
face and rasterised by another. #170 broke the rule by writing a replacement's
file NAME into the proprietary position. This does the opposite: it points the
proprietary family's row at the position its replacement already occupies.
Nothing is renamed, no file is copied, one file stays one download.

Two more things had to be true, both learned by measuring:

- A family the fallback table routes to needs a record in
  `g_fonts_selection_bin`, or the matcher cannot find it by name and lands in
  the same shifted-glyph failure. That blob was treated as unmodifiable; its
  reader is in sdk-all.js, so bin/lib/selection-bin.mjs now implements the
  layout both ways. It round-trips the shipped bytes exactly, and a record
  rebuilt from a font's own OS/2 + head + post equals the vendor generator's
  record for all 188 catalog files that map one-to-one.
- The CJK faces have to be TrueType. The pan-CJK OTFs render perfectly in the
  editor and export to PDF as nothing at all: x2t embeds no glyphs for a
  CFF-flavoured face, so the Chinese comes out blank and the Latin survives.
  They are now static instances of the Noto Sans/Serif SC variable fonts,
  subset -- sans to the whole CJK repertoire because every fallback range
  points at it, serif to GB2312 because it backs the names a document asks for.

What that buys, beyond the licensing: Chinese and Japanese come out of one
typeface instead of four, 48 Chinese families gain a drawn bold instead of a
smeared one, and Arabic, Hebrew, Armenian, Georgian, Cyrillic Supplement,
Syriac and Thaana get faces that actually cover them -- Calibri had been
carrying five of those alone, and Syriac and Thaana had never been covered.
public/fonts/ goes from 327 MB to 184 MB.

Also fixes an existing defect: PDF_FONT_MANIFEST still named slots 267-270,
which #174 removed and never restored, so Chinese in an exported PDF has been
blank since. The slots exist again and two cases pin them.

Tests, each reverse-validated:

- font-catalog-licensing: every file's own name table must show an open
  license; the invariant above; fallback routes must point at faces that carry
  the characters. Re-applying #170's mistake turns it red with the position it
  broke.
- font-selection-bin: byte-exact round trip, record rebuild, every routed
  family indexed. Dropping the appended records turns it red.
- font-substitution (E2E): a substituted name and the open family behind it
  share a position, so the two renderings must be pixel-identical. Healthy
  0.00-0.06%, broken 0.8-1.0%.
- pdf-cjk-export (E2E): a Chinese-only document exported to PDF must keep its
  ink. With the CFF faces it reports 3.14% in the editor and 0.05% in the PDF.

Full suite: 992 unit, 122 E2E, green.

perf(history): verify the adaptive interval actually backs off on slow devices

The duty-cycle rule was designed for phones and measured only on a desktop --
the one claim it makes was the one thing not checked. bin/export-benchmark.mjs
can now throttle the CPU through the DevTools protocol (4x and 6x standing in
for a mid-range and a low-end phone), which tests the claim without owning the
hardware.

It holds, and the back-off is continuous rather than stepped:

  docx, one paragraph    40 ms -> 30 s | 197 ms -> 59 s  | 335 ms -> 101 s
  docx, 2000 paragraphs  87 ms -> 30 s | 315 ms -> 95 s  | 495 ms -> 149 s
  xlsx, 20k rows        141 ms -> 42 s | 573 ms -> 172 s | 896 ms -> 180 s

Worst case on a low-end phone is a 100-180 s window, still tighter than
Office AutoRecover's ten-minute default. A single export there costs 896 ms of
main thread for the heaviest workbook, which is felt -- but spread over a 3
minute interval it is still 0.33% of the session. That is the argument for a
duty cycle over a fixed number: the device decides how long a stall lasts, we
decide what fraction of the time is spent stalling.

Also measured what the storage layer costs on the editor's critical path, since
it is imported statically: /history is its own entry (23 kB, 6.7 kB gzipped)
and never reaches the editor, and removing the session call entirely moves the
total gzipped JS by -774 bytes, i.e. inside chunk-splitting noise. A few kB is
not worth an async boundary; noted with the limits of that measurement.

fix(editor): move a tab off an older build by itself, and stop flashing the home panel

Two things a user hit after the font sweep shipped.

**Refreshing did not get them the new build.** A deploy whose vendored tree
changed leaves its worker waiting -- activating it deletes the caches the
outgoing build is still reading. The page promotes it only when no document is
open, and the landing page only when no editor window is open at all, so
someone who goes straight to /editor and keeps a document open is never asked:
reloading serves the old build back. With that build's fonts deleted from the
origin by the same deploy, their screen stayed garbled for a day after the
revert had shipped.

The page can fix this itself, because the navigation is network-first: the HTML
and bundle a stale tab loads are already the new ones, only the vendored tree
underneath is not. healStaleController() promotes the waiting worker and
reloads once, at boot, silently -- no prompt, at most once per tab
(sessionStorage), never over unsaved edits. No interruption was the ask.

Deciding *when* to do that took three attempts, and the two failures are worth
keeping:

- The vendored editor registers a worker of its own into the same scope from
  inside its iframe (/document_editor_service_worker.js, an empty stub here).
  A scope holds one registration, so the script alternates and `waiting` is
  almost always non-null -- and whoever promotes it can hand the whole origin
  to an empty worker. Both promotion paths now check the script URL.
- Asking the *controller* which build it is looked reasonable and was not: a
  busy worker misses the timeout, silence read as "it is old", and tabs
  reloaded themselves mid-run. The full suite failed 2 of 138 on this branch
  while the same machine ran the baseline green; disabling the wiring made it
  122 green and two minutes faster. The evidence is local instead: sw.js names
  its runtime cache after the vendor hash, so "does this browser hold that
  build's cache" answers the question without a conversation. Silence now
  means do nothing.

**The home-state panel flashed during load.** It is built visible and only
hidden once a document takes over, and `?saved=` adds two dynamic imports
before that -- long enough on a cold load to read "View/Edit Document / New
Word / New Excel / New PowerPoint" under the spinner. When the URL already
names a document, the panel is never painted.

Tests, each reverse-validated: sw-silent-update.spec.ts deploys a second build
by rewriting the vendor stamp in the served sw.js and requires the next load to
be on it with no notice element; entry-paths samples the panel from first paint;
unit cases cover the script-URL guard, the cache-name evidence and the
once-per-tab heal.

fix(editor): a missing translation must not become a document error

Reported in Korean: opening a blank document showed the vendor's modal
"An error occurred while working with the document. Use the 'Download
as' option to save a backup copy" -- before typing anything. Reproduced
in a production build; only ko, and every time.

The cause is a translation gap. `DE.Views.Statusbar.tipMultiplePages` is
in en.json and not in ko.json, and unlike most strings it has no default
in the component's own source, so the property is `undefined`. The status

document error, and the user gets a modal telling them to save a backup
of a document they have not written yet.

This is not one bad file: all 44 non-English locales are short against
en.json, from 1 key to 3167. Korean simply lost the lottery of which gap
reaches a tooltip setter. So there are two defences:

1. bin/locale-fill.mjs backfills, from en.json, every key missing in the
   locales this site is translated into -- 17 files, ~113 KB, keeping the
   vendor's minified formatting so the tree does not grow by 25 KB a file.
   bin/build.sh runs it before the vendor tree is hashed into
   VENDOR_VERSION, and test/unit/vendor-locale.test.ts fails when it has
   not been run (which is what a vendor upgrade will do).
2. Guard 11 (guards/hint-fallback.ts) makes `updateHint(undefined)` a
   no-op. That covers the other 38 locales, which `?locale=` can still
   select, and whatever the next upgrade breaks.

An English tooltip is a blemish. A modal error on an empty document is
someone deciding this editor cannot be trusted with their file.

fix(sw): whoever promotes the waiting worker owns the reload

CI kept failing the @serial silent-update case with a 90s timeout, and the
screenshot was a blank white page. The trace says why: the editor iframe's own
document request came back -1, and nothing retries it.

Activating a worker terminates the outgoing one, and every fetch it still had
in flight fails -- including that iframe navigation. That is survivable only
because a reload follows. The reload did not follow.

promoteWaitingWorker runs the moment register() resolves, which on the editor
route is a few hundred milliseconds before the editor instance exists. It
therefore sees "no document open" and promotes. By the time controllerchange
arrives the document is open, shouldReloadOnControllerChange asks the same
question again, gets the other answer, and refuses -- with the page already
torn in half. wireServiceWorkerUpdates was dropping promoteWaitingWorker's
return value, so the page never knew it had asked for the swap itself.

It now reports it. index.ts keeps one flag for both promotion paths (the
ordinary update and the stale-build heal), renamed promotedFromThisTab, and a
tab that asked for the swap reloads regardless of what is open -- unsaved
edits still veto. Refusing the reload does not undo the swap; it only leaves
the reader on a blank editor.

Reverse-verified: stashing lib/sw-update.ts and index.ts turns all four new
unit cases red. sw-silent-update and sw-warm pass locally.

fix(sw): do not promote a worker while a document is on its way

The first half of this change turned every promotion into a reload, which the
Cloudflare Pages E2E caught: autosave-recovery's reload case went red on the
shard and stayed red on retry, while the same shard was green on a branch
without it.

CLAUDE.md already says why. A worker waiting is not a new version: the
vendored editor registers a worker of its own into this scope from inside the
iframe, so the scope's script alternates and ours sits in `waiting` on almost
every editor load with no new build anywhere. "Refuse the reload when a
document is open" was doubling as the brake on that. Removing it made those
routine swaps reload the page every time.

So the other half: a page that is about to open a document does not promote at
all. hasOpenDocument() reads the store, which fills a few hundred milliseconds
after register() resolves -- the URL knows sooner, and ?new= / ?file= / ?src= /
?open= / ?saved= all say a document is coming. Embed mode counts too, and for a
stronger reason: the host can push a document at any moment, and the reload
would throw away something the host page owns.

A worker left waiting on those routes is the case the silent heal exists for,
and that path checks isUnseenBuild() first, so the vendor's worker shuffling
cannot fool it.

Reverse-verified: stashing lib/sw-update.ts turns the three new
documentIsExpected cases red. autosave-recovery (all three), sw-silent-update
and sw-warm pass locally -- the reload case being the one that was red with
only the first half.

Still red in CI, same case, same blank page. Lining up the network timeline
says why both earlier attempts missed:

  25.68  the reload's document, served by the old worker
  25.74  GET /sw.js -- bytes differ, install starts

misses exactly the cases that happen; promotedFromThisTab and the onPromoted
plumbing are gone.

The condition that is left is the one that was always the real one: unsaved

fix(sw): reload on a controller change only when the build really changed

The previous commit reloaded on any controller change, and three E2E shards
said no. A controller changing is routine: the vendored editor registers a
worker of its own into this scope, ours is re-installed and left waiting on
ordinary loads, and the browser activates it by itself at the next navigation
-- same build, same caches, nothing behind it. Measured at 80ms into a plain
reload of a fresh profile, which is why sw-vendor-cache-first died with
"Execution context was destroyed" in the middle of its probe.

So the condition is two things, and both are load-bearing:

  - the new controller is a build this browser has not been running, judged
    the way healStaleController judges it -- by the runtime cache, named after
    the vendor tree's content. The cache names are snapshotted at boot: read
    them when the swap happens and the incoming worker has already created its
    own, and asking the outgoing worker instead is asking something a swap may
    already have terminated;
  - and there are no unsaved edits.

Not "is a document open", which is what left a torn page unrepaired, and not
"did this tab ask for the swap", which misses the cases that actually happen.

Reverse-verified in both directions, locally, which the earlier attempts could
not manage: pinning isNewBuild false turns sw-silent-update red, pinning it
true turns sw-vendor-cache-first red. With the real value, sw-silent-update,
sw-vendor-cache-first, sw-warm, autosave-recovery and font-cache pass -- eight
cases.

Tried and dropped: having sw.js skip its install-time takeover when a core
cache under this build's name already exists, so that a same-build re-install
stops swapping the controller mid-load. Its unit case reverse-verified, but
the local suite is green with and without it, and it has a real cost -- a
rollback to a build this browser has run would no longer be delivered, which
is the font revert's own scenario. Unproven benefit, delicate path, out.

fix(sw): do not let a busy worker's silence cancel the reload that repairs a torn page

A blank editor in CI, on the silent-heal case. The trace says the controller
did change (the test's own three-second VERSION question to the new worker was
answered), the third editor boot started and died before a single guard
installed -- and no fourth boot ever began. The reload that repairs a page the
swap tore in half never happened.

What cancelled it was the one-second question in isUnseenBuild. A worker
answers VERSION from its message handler, which it cannot run while it is
busy, and it is busiest in exactly that moment: just activated, terminating
the worker it replaced, with the page refetching a vendor tree it has not
cached. The silence was read as "nothing new", so isNewBuild came back false
and the tab stayed blank until the test gave up.

This file already learned that lesson once -- "a worker under load does not
answer within a timeout" -- but on the promotion side, which was moved to
cache evidence. The controllerchange side kept asking, and here a wrong answer
is not a wasted reload: it is a white page with no way out but a manual one.

So: askVersionPatiently, three tries of two seconds. Silence still decides,
it just cannot decide early.

Not the judgement conditions, deliberately. "Is a document open" is already
known to be the wrong one, and "unsaved changes" was not the cause -- the boot
that died was a fresh page load with the dirty flag false. Not cache evidence
either: a page torn mid-boot may not have completed one vendor request, so the
incoming build has no runtime cache to be seen by.

Reverse-verified: with askVersion back in place, exactly one of the new cases
fails and the other 52 pass.

fix(safari): hand the picked file over in a shape IndexedDB will actually keep

The static landing pages carry no app bundle, so "open a file" goes through
IndexedDB: the page stashes what the visitor picked and the editor takes it out
on boot. Safari will not structured-clone a File or a Blob into a store, and
the way it says so is to accept the put and then fail the transaction with a
null error. The handoff read that as "IndexedDB unavailable", took its fallback
of dropping `open=local` from the URL, and the visitor arrived at an empty
editor holding nothing of the document they had just chosen. Five of the eleven
red cases in the cross-browser nightly were this one bug, and it is shipped.

The File still goes in first, because storing it costs nothing: it is a
reference to bytes already on disk and the editor opens it with
createObjectURL without ever reading it. But the write is confirmed by reading
it back, since "the put did not throw" is not the same as "the file is in
there" -- fake-indexeddb keeps an empty object in its place, quietly, and an
engine that failed that way would reproduce the same symptom past any check of
the write alone. Only when the store will not keep a File are the bytes read
and stored instead; doing that unconditionally would put a stall with no
feedback between the file dialog and the navigation, and on a large enough
file `arrayBuffer()` rejects -- landing on the exact empty editor this is here
to prevent. The reader accepts both shapes, a bare File included, so a landing
page cached before this change still hands off.

The landing page's warm-up had a second Safari defect. It runs for the whole
time the visitor reads, so a multi-MB fetch is nearly always open when they
finally click -- and a request the BROWSER cancels at unload is reported as an
error nobody can catch: an uncaught "Fetch API cannot load <url> due to access
control checks" on WebKit, one line per queued file. Probed: fetch() returns a
promise normally and a rejection handler IS attached; the document dies before
the microtask can run. Firefox blames the service worker instead ("intercepted
the request and encountered an unexpected error"), and that one is not fixable
from the worker either -- the same line appears whether sw.js answers from
cache, with a synthetic 504, or with Response.error().

So the warm-up cancels its own requests at beforeunload, while the page is
still alive to handle the rejection. pagehide alone was measured and is too
late. Because beforeunload also fires for navigations that never happen, any
sign the document is still in use picks the warm-up back up -- deliberately not
a timer, which a slow navigation would let fire just before unload and restart
the very requests we cancelled.

Four defects in the harness, each of which had been failing or flaking nightly:

- L0 could not see what a test allowed. Firefox hands `console.error(someError)`
  to the driver as the bare word "Error", and by the time the argument could be
  resolved the frame that logged it is gone. open-retry allowed the fault it
  injects by message and matched nothing. Errors are now stringified at the
  call site, on every engine.
- Firefox's wording for a cancelled request joins Chromium's net::ERR_ on the
  console allowlist, with the three falsifications in the comment.
- landing-prefetch polled the Cache API at Playwright's default 100 ms, which
  starved the worker's own put of the last (9.4 MB) core file: 7 of 8 for the
  whole three-minute budget on Firefox, seconds at one poll per second.
- save-to-file needs OPFS writable streams to stub its picker with, and WebKit
  has the handles but not the streams (createWritable rejects for every payload
  shape). Skipped on a capability probe, not a browser name, so it starts
  running by itself if that changes.

And two races that had been flaking for weeks: `page.goto('/?embed=1')`
resolves on the landing page, before the redirect to /editor that the embed
params trigger, so an evaluate started in the gap dies with the context; and
waitForEditorReady died the same way when lib/sw-update.ts silently moved the
tab onto a build this browser had not run before, which on a cold profile is
every first visit -- a shipped feature working, reported as a failure. It now
starts over on the new document, inside the same deadline.

feat(i18n): the language menu is a list of links, not a form field

It looked wrong in four ways at once and they all had the same cause: the menu
was an <r-select>, which is a combobox -- a form field -- standing in a row of
bare navigation links.

A form field is built to hold a fixed width with its label at one end and its
caret at the other, because its options vary in length and the layout has to
stay still. So the globe could only sit outside the box, the 132px width left
~70px of dead space between "EN" and the caret, and the abbreviation existed to
save room in the first place. The panel landed left of its own trigger for a
related reason: aligned to the leading edge it overflowed the viewport and the
shift middleware pulled it back -- 33px clear of the trigger, measured.

WAI-ARIA's own guidance is that a menu of navigation links is a disclosure: a
button with aria-expanded over a list of links. Not a menu, and certainly not a
combobox. So it is one now -- ranui's <r-popover> for the open/close behaviour,
and `<a href lang hreflang>` for the entries.

What that buys, beyond the four symptoms going away:

- Every language is named in its own words. English was the one abbreviation
  among six endonyms, and this menu's whole audience is readers who cannot read
  the page it sits on -- "EN" is legible only to someone who already reads
  English.
- `lang` on each entry, so a screen reader pronounces 日本語 as Japanese instead
  of reading it with the current page's phonetics.
- Real links: middle-clickable, copyable, crawlable, and they work with
  JavaScript off. The script is down to writing the cookie that carries the
  choice into /editor and /history, which are one app and resolve their language
  from ?locale= → cookie → localStorage → browser.
- The check marks the current entry and the background is left to hover. Both
  used to be near-identical greys, so the current row read as merely hovered.
- 84KB less on every landing page: select.iife.js is 152KB against 68KB for
  popover + content, and r-select had no other user on the site.
- The phone bar keeps the GitHub link. It used to be dropped to make room for a
  trigger wide enough to hold "Português"; the trigger now drops the language
  name instead and keeps the globe.

Two things worth knowing before touching this again, both in the exploration
note: `::part(dropdown)` cannot reach this panel (it is portalled to <body> as
its own r-dropdown), and a document-level click delegate never hears the menu
because r-popover stops propagation at the panel -- the listeners go on the
links themselves.

The menu's order is an explicit list rather than a sort: `localeCompare` answers
according to the host's ICU data, so a sorted menu could come out in a different
order locally than in CI. A test pins that the list covers every locale, since
forgetting it would silently drop a language from every menu on the site.

Reverse-checked: dropping the `lang` attribute fails 156 cases; putting
`placement` back to `bottom` fails the right-alignment case by 24px.

refactor(i18n): build the language menu with ranui's DOM, not string concatenation

The first version concatenated the markup by hand, on the assumption that
`ranui/builder` needs a browser DOM and this is a node build script. That
assumption was never checked, and it is wrong: the builder falls back to ranui's
own DOM mock when there is no `document`, so the ecosystem rule -- construct DOM
with the builder, not by hand -- applies here exactly as it does in the browser.

Using `View()`/`Div()` directly then ran into a second thing. They pick between
the mock and `document.createElement` by environment, and this file renders the
same pages in two: node for the real build, jsdom under vitest. A real document
lowercases the attribute names of an element made with `createElement`, so
`viewBox` came back as `viewbox` -- SVG reads it case-sensitively, so the icon
would not have rendered -- and the two environments produced different bytes for
the same page, which fails `check()` (the test that a fresh render would not
change a committed page) permanently.

So this uses `HTMLElementMock`, which `ranui/builder` exports, through two small
helpers. Same behaviour in both environments, and attributes and text are
escaped on the way out -- the part hand-written HTML gets wrong quietly. What
the rule is actually after is intact: no concatenated markup, no hand-rolled
`escapeHtml` at each interpolation.

It also turned up a real gap upstream: the builders have no `createElementNS`
path at all (`utils/builder/core.ts` only calls `document.createElement`), so in
a real browser they cannot construct SVG -- `View('svg')` yields an
`HTMLUnknownElement` with lowercased attributes. Anyone using them for an icon
will hit it. Noted in the exploration for a follow-up in chaxus/ran.

2870 unit tests and the language-menu e2e pass; the generated `viewBox` keeps
its casing, and the jsdom render now matches the committed page byte for byte.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(a11y): the language switcher is one control, not a button inside a popup

Found while auditing the project against the ecosystem rules, not by a test.

The trigger was a `<button>` nested inside `<r-popover>`, which reads as the
obvious shape for a disclosure. But r-popover puts `tabindex`, `aria-haspopup`
and `aria-expanded` on *itself* -- its design assumes the host is the trigger.
So the control took two tab stops and split its information in half:

  r-popover      tabindex=0, aria-expanded="false", no role, no name
  button inside  aria-label="Language", never reports being open

A screen reader therefore never gets "Language, collapsed" as one thing. It
meets an anonymous popup, then a button that does not say it is open.

`role="button"` and the name go on the host now, and the inner element is a
`<span>` -- it was only ever the row of icon, label and caret. One tab stop, with
the name and the state on the same element, which is the shape ARIA's disclosure
pattern asks for. The focus ring moves with it.

Reverse-checked: restoring the nested button fails the new case with
`Expected 1, Received 2` tab stops. There is also a keyboard case now (Tab to
it, Enter to open, Escape to close), which nothing covered before.
